Senses.PreferredTarget: the chick pecks and the hen taps at the same instant
AlternateTargets: pecking and tapping at the same instant
Senses.Explanation: Literally, the chick pecks from inside the shell while the hen taps from outside at the same instant. The phrase occurs 221 times in 71 allowlisted texts. A later record defines the image graph by graph: the chick pecks, the mother taps, and neither precedes the other. In the Chan record it names a matched teacher-student exchange and is extended into an 'eye,' a 'function,' and a 'responsive mechanism.' Nanyuan's repeatedly quoted public interview distinguishes possessing the eye from possessing the function, then says that when adepts meet they do not peck and tap: doing so at the same instant misses it. Yuanwu applies the phrase to Fayan's answer 'you are Huichao' and to teachers who respond to circumstances. This deployment as a technical description of timing in public exchange is the corpus-specific bend of the hatching image.
Senses.Note: The sources themselves preserve a tension: one defines simultaneity through the chick-and-hen image, while the Nanyuan case says adepts who enact the named peck-and-tap miss it. This entry reports both formulations without resolving their intent.

Senses.Explanation: Literally, 'sit across and cut off.' The compound occurs 3,034 times in 339 allowed texts and takes concrete grammatical objects. Yuanwu answers a monk with 'sit across and cut off the tongues of everyone under heaven' (坐斷天下人舌頭), says that 'emerging and submerging are all sat across and cut off' (頭出頭沒悉皆坐斷), and records a monk's conclusion, 'then one sits across and cuts off the ten directions' (坐斷十方). Blue Cliff commentary says a master's half-phrase 'naturally sits across and cuts off the tongues of everyone under heaven' (自然坐斷天下人舌頭). The Ancestral Guidelines Collection says 'sit across and bar the critical crossing; do not let ordinary or holy pass' (坐斷要津，不通凡聖), and elsewhere, 'sit across and cut off the crown of Vairocana; do not receive Śākyamuni's text' (坐斷毗盧頂，不稟釋迦文). Other frequent objects include past and present, a thousand distinctions, the road's intersection, and the heads of buddhas. The verb is therefore transitive and spatially forceful in the corpus; it is not a term for seated quiet.
Senses.Note: Required formula searches yielded a handful of grammatical instances but no stable self-definition. The repeated objects establish the translation: tongues, ten directions, the critical crossing, a crown, and past/present are what the texts say are barred or cut off.

Senses.Explanation: Literally, sit and Chan. The compound occurs 1,121 times in 244 allowlisted Chinese Chan texts. It can name literal seated activity in the hall: a monastic rule says the assembly sits facing inward as in ordinary sitting Chan and turns outward when the drum sounds. The Platform Record asks, 'What is sitting Chan?' and gives its own graph-by-graph definition: toward all good and bad circumstances outside, thoughts not arising is called 'sitting'; inwardly seeing one's own nature unmoved is called 'Chan.' The wider record also preserves direct critiques. In the Nanyue tile case, Huairang asks what Daoyi seeks by sitting Chan and says, 'If polishing a tile cannot make a mirror, how could sitting Chan make a buddha?' A verse addressed to those attached to sitting Chan asks why prolonged sitting is needed. A raised Linji exchange says that the monks in his hall neither read texts nor sit Chan. These records do not present one uniform predicate beyond the literal compound.
Senses.Note: No exact mind-king/seat equation exists in the allowlist: 'mind-king seat,' 'seat of the mind-king,' 'sitting is the mind-king,' and 'the mind-king sits securely' all have zero hits. The closest explicit witness says that the mind-king is free and easy and then asks, 'Why restrain thoughts and sit Chan?'—a critique, not a seat definition. The contiguous string 'sit Chan seat' occurs 15 times in 14 texts, but in passages such as 'although seated on the Chan seat' it parses as the verb 'sit' plus the noun 'Chan seat'; this boundary does not redefine sitting Chan as furniture.

Senses.Explanation: Literally, bind or establish, and regulation or restriction. In Chan records the term labels the formal beginning of a bounded communal period and also functions as a verb for beginning it. It occurs 2,026 times in 255 allowlisted texts. Records repeatedly mark a discourse or small talk as delivered at this beginning, contrast it with release from the restriction, and identify the date: one record calls the fifteenth day of the tenth month the restriction and the fifteenth day of the first month its release; another describes the interval from the former date to the Lantern Festival. A tea talk parses the two graphs as joining companions of one purpose and holding a wild mind in check. Individual answers remain concrete: asked what the restriction is, one master says, 'Return to your place.'
Senses.Note: The term overlaps with beginning the summer session, but the corpus also attests a winter restriction, so 'summer session' is too narrow as the head gloss. Release from the restriction is the consistent opposite. The corpus has 136 instances of the compact heading 'restriction-period discourse' and 20 of 'restriction-period small talk.'
